client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on my chest all the time, and I can't shake it. But honestly, what's weighing on me even more is watching my mom fall apart and not knowing what to say or do to help her — I feel completely useless, and I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is so heavy — grief for your grandmother *and* the pain of watching your mom struggle, all while feeling like you should somehow be doing more. That sense of helplessness around the people we love can actually hurt even more than our own grief sometimes. I'm glad you're here, and I'm curious — when you say you feel useless with your mom, what does "helping her" look like in your mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess in my mind, "helping her" means being able to actually fix her sadness, like if I call enough or say the right things, I can pull her out of it. But no matter what I do, she still sounds so lost on the phone, and I hang up feeling like I failed somehow. It's this constant loop of trying and feeling like it's never enough.
therapist: That loop you're describing — trying, hoping, hanging up deflated — sounds exhausting, and I notice there's something almost breathless in how you're carrying all of this, like you're running hard just to stay in place. The belief that it's *your job* to fix her grief is such a heavy weight to place on yourself, and it's worth gently questioning — is it actually possible for one person to "fix" another's sadness, even with all the love in the world? I wonder what it might feel like to redefine "helping" as simply *being there*, rather than needing to change the outcome.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right — no one can really fix someone else's grief. But it doesn't feel that simple, because she's my mom and she's been struggling since my dad died, and if I don't try to help her, who will? The idea of just "being there" without actually changing anything feels like giving up, like I'm letting her down all over again.
therapist: The weight in your voice as you say that tells me this fear of letting her down runs really deep — this isn't just about grief, it sounds like you've been holding yourself responsible for her wellbeing for a long time, maybe even before your grandmother passed. That word "again" caught my attention — "letting her down *all over again*" — can you tell me more about what that "again" means to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Yeah... the "again" is... it's a lot to unpack. I think the first time I really felt like I let my mom down was when I was maybe sixteen, she was going through a really hard stretch after my dad left, and I just kind of... withdrew. I was dealing with my own stuff and I wasn't there for her the way she needed me to be, and I've never really forgiven myself for that. So now, with my grandmother gone and my mom falling apart again, it feels like history repeating itself, like I'm making the same mistake I made back then.
therapist: That sixteen-year-old who withdrew wasn't failing her mother — she was a teenager in pain, doing the only thing she knew how to do to survive. It makes so much sense that this moment is pulling you back there, but I want to gently offer this: carrying unforgiveness toward your younger self for thirty years is an enormous burden, and it may be quietly shaping how hard you're pushing yourself right now. What do you think you would say to that sixteen-year-old girl if she were sitting here with us?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think I'd want to tell her that she was doing her best, but honestly, even saying that out loud right now feels almost... wrong, like I don't quite believe I deserve to give her that kind of grace. There's this voice in my head that immediately says, "but your mom needed you and you just hid in your room," and I can't seem to get past that. I know logically what you're saying makes sense, but thirty years of telling myself a different story is hard to just... set down.
therapist: The way you said that — quickly, softly, like you were almost trying to slip past your own words — tells me this touches something really tender in you. That critical voice has had thirty years of practice, so of course it's loud and fast to interrupt the moment you try to offer yourself any kindness. I'm curious — whose voice does it sound like, that one that says "but your mom needed you"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly... it sounds like my own voice, but I think it learned from hers. My mom used to say things like "I just need you to be there for me" whenever I tried to do something for myself, and after a while I stopped being able to tell the difference between her needs and my guilt. It's strange to hear you name it like that, because part of me still wants to defend her — she was struggling, she really did need help.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that over time, her needs and your guilt became so intertwined that you lost the thread back to yourself, and that's not a small thing to recognize. And I notice you want to defend her even now, which speaks to how much you love her, but holding both things can be true: she was struggling *and* the weight she placed on you was more than a child should have had to carry. What's it like to sit with both of those being true at the same time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's... uncomfortable, honestly. Like, part of me wants to just pick one — either she was struggling and that explains everything, or it was too much for me to carry — because holding both at the same time feels like I'm betraying her somehow. I don't know if I'm allowed to feel burdened by someone I also love that deeply.
therapist: The words you're choosing are careful and measured, but there's something in your voice that sounds quieter, more fragile — like this is costing you more than you're quite letting on. That question — "am I *allowed* to feel burdened by someone I love?" — is such an important one, and I want to sit with it for a moment, because somewhere along the way it sounds like you learned that loving someone meant you had to make yourself very small. Where do you think you learned that love and burden couldn't exist in the same space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... I think maybe it was just always modeled that way. Like, my mom never complained, ever, even when things were really hard, and I guess I just absorbed this idea that if you truly love someone, you just... carry it quietly and you don't make it about yourself. But hearing you say it like that, that I "made myself small," I don't know if I fully buy that framing — it feels more like I was just trying to be a good person.
therapist: It's interesting — you're pushing back on the framing a little, but your voice sounds quieter and more subdued than your words, like part of you is still sitting with something that landed. "Being a good person" and "making yourself small" might not be as different as they feel right now — what if the way you learned to be good *required* the smallness? I'm curious what it brings up for you to consider that those two things might have been quietly tied together all along.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's... I don't know, that actually kind of stopped me for a second. Like, if being good meant staying quiet and not taking up space, then every time I tried to want something for myself it probably felt like I was being selfish or bad. I guess I never really thought about it that way, but it's a little unsettling to sit with because it means a lot of what I thought was just "being considerate" might have actually been me disappearing.
therapist: That word — "disappearing" — is such a profound one, and the fact that it came from you, not from me, tells me something important just clicked into place. What you're describing is a lifetime of confusing self-erasure with virtue, and that's a genuinely unsettling thing to see clearly, maybe for the first time. I want to ask you gently — what feels most tender about that realization right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what feels most tender is... realizing that I've been doing it for so long that I don't even know what I actually want anymore. Like, I've spent so much time making myself smaller so other people would be comfortable, and now when I try to think about what *I* need, there's just this blank, hollow feeling. It's almost scarier than the loneliness itself, because at least loneliness is something I recognize.
therapist: That hollow feeling you're describing — not knowing what you want after a lifetime of setting yourself aside — is one of the most disorienting things a person can discover about themselves, and it makes complete sense that it frightens you. The loneliness is familiar, but this blankness feels like standing in a room you've never been in before. I want you to know that the fact you can *name* that hollow space means you're already beginning to find your way back to yourself — and I'm wondering, is there anything, even something small or fleeting, that has ever felt like it belonged just to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
